prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in Romanian poetry and fiction, that turns memory, the body and dream into an encyclopedic metaphysical cosmos

statement.case_for: After reading the colleagues' openings, I keep Cărtărescu first. The case rests on voice, scale and the architecture of the whole oeuvre. In the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid, the body, childhood memory, dream and metaphysical speculation are built into one recognisable imaginative system, in sentences of great density. Public knowledge also places the work in a long lineage of visionary and modernist writing, and it does not read as derivative of it. His poetic origins and his essayistic side seem to feed the prose rather than sit beside it. His career has run from the 1980s to large late works, which suggests cumulative development rather than a single breakthrough. I assess this under the common criteria of distinct voice, linguistic and formal achievement, sustained quality, imaginative depth and significance. I do not weigh it by how many colleagues rank him highly. Can Xue remains a very strong competitor on distinctiveness and formal uncompromisingness. I place Cărtărescu first because his project seems to me to vary more in scale and register while keeping its identity.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that the quality of the long late volumes may not be uniformly sustained. Several colleagues, including Carlberg, Palm and Mattson, raise the risk of repetition or excess of motif in very large books. I cannot dismiss this. Prose of this ornate density also depends heavily on Romanian lexical and syntactic richness. My judgment, like that of the committee, is therefore mediated by translation, and the poetry and earlier fiction are thinly covered. If the committee concludes that recurrence in his work is exhaustion rather than architecture, the case weakens considerably.

responses.point: Palm ranks Can Xue first for an anti-realist, dream-logic project sustained over decades. She sets it apart from conventional realist or national-allegory frames. She also notes that the work may seem repetitive or hermetic and that its sustained quality needs more checking.
responses.response: I agree with the distinctiveness claim and with the caveat. The question of whether a method that unvarying gives range or only intensity decides how I rank her against Cărtărescu. I hold Can Xue as my first alternative. The difference for me is small. Cărtărescu's work seems to build a more varied imaginative edifice from related materials, across prose and poetry and across registers from the intimate to the cosmic. That is a judgment from public knowledge and translations. I do not claim a verified reading of the Chinese original, and we should treat Palm's caution about corpus coverage as applying to both candidates.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Can Xue first for a rigorously maintained dream logic. She places Cărtărescu third and flags translation difficulty and possible critical debate about excess and repetition in the longer volumes.
responses.response: The repetition concern is the most serious objection to my first choice, and I do not wish to wave it away. I would separate recurrence of motif used as structure, as in a trilogy that circles one body and one memory, from recurrence as thinning. Which of the two applies in the later volumes of Solenoid and after is something I can only judge partly, through translation. Carlberg's own acknowledgment that Can Xue's long works may divide readers on sustained quality parallels my doubt, so I do not think the two cases separate cleanly on this criterion. I would ask the committee to test the late long books of both writers on the page.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita first for long poetic sequences that turn collective suffering under dictatorship into memorial form. He warns that the non-textual interventions must not be allowed to carry the case.
responses.response: I take the force of Zurita's project seriously. I rank him sixth, not higher, for the reasons Olsson himself names. Poetry loses most in translation, and the landscape-scale works fall largely outside the text, which makes the citation hard to confine to the poems. If his case is argued strictly from the verbal achievement of Purgatory and Anteparadise, it becomes more persuasive. Olsson's insistence that the political setting not substitute for literary merit is correct. I would also apply it symmetrically to other candidates whose subject matter carries historical weight.

responses.point: Mattson, like me, ranks Cărtărescu first. She stresses coherence across volumes and across prose and poetry, and she places Can Xue second.
responses.response: I agree on coherence, but shared first place does not strengthen the literary argument, and I would not use it that way. Her own caveats are the ones I would press: ornate sentences and density of imagery may not carry equally in every language, and the poetry and earlier prose are thinly known to us. I would add that the committee should not credit a coherence we have seen mainly in the major novels to the whole body of work without checking the poetry. I would be open to a citation that names the novels as the centre and the poetry as a foundation rather than an equal pillar.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Can Xue first and Robinson second. She values Robinson's moral interiority and control of cadence, and she worries about formal monotony in Can Xue's method.
responses.response: I accept that Robinson's sentence-level achievement is high and that her essays add a second strand, and I respect her second place on Swärd's list. My difficulty is breadth. The fiction is compact and the formal range is narrower than in the more radical candidates, which Swärd also acknowledges. I would ask what citation could state a significance larger than one deeply explored world. On monotony, I share the worry about Can Xue, and I think that is why the uniformity of method versus range question must be treated as open for her, as it is for Cărtărescu's repetition.

uncertainties: Whether the late long volumes of Cărtărescu's oeuvre sustain their density and quality, or whether recurrence of motif becomes exhaustion, cannot be settled from the supplied evidence.
My assessment of Cărtărescu's prose, and of Can Xue's, is mediated by translation. I have not independently verified any text or the quality of the Swedish and English versions.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and earlier fiction is thin in my knowledge, so the claim that poetry and prose form one coherent project is partly inferred.
The relative weight of Can Xue's consistent method against Cărtărescu's wider scale is a close judgment and could reasonably go the other way.
Comparing a poet, hybrid writers and novelists under common criteria remains imprecise, especially for work with visual or non-textual components.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own literary practice is set in Central Europe, but that is context and not a recusal ground or evidence of a preference. The profile shows no connection to any shortlisted writer.
